prompt.context_jp: 高層ビルの窓が夕日を映し、駅前には家路を急ぐ人々の波が途切れることなく続いていた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 高層ビルの窓___夕日を映し、駅前には家路を急ぐ人々の波が途切れることなく続いていた。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle that fits this opening description.

feedback.correct_en: The scene is being set from scratch — the windows are new information the narrator is painting in. が introduces this fresh visual element inside a descriptive clause.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would frame 'the windows' as an already-known topic being commented on, which doesn't fit a scene-opening description. を would require a transitive verb targeting the windows.

contrast_examples.jp: 窓が光を反射している。
contrast_examples.en: The windows (new to the scene) reflect the light.
As for the windows, they face south. (topic)

prompt.context_jp: 人混みの中を、黒いスーツに身を包んだ一人の女がまっすぐに歩いていく。
prompt.prompt_jp: 人混みの中を、黒いスーツに身を包んだ一人の女___まっすぐに歩いていく。
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the particle that introduces this mysterious woman for the first time.

feedback.correct_en: This is the woman's first appearance in the story. が presents her as new information — a figure the reader is just now noticing in the crowd.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would imply she had already been established as the topic. Since she's being introduced here for the first time, が is natural.

contrast_examples.jp: 一人の女が歩いてきた。
contrast_examples.en: A woman came walking (newly noticed).

contrast_examples.jp: その女は三軒家だった。
contrast_examples.en: That woman (already introduced) was Sangenya.

prompt.context_jp: 屋代が壁の成績表の前で足を止める場面。
prompt.prompt_jp: 一番上に並んでいるの___、いつものように足立聡の名前だった。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle that frames the subject as the topic being described.

feedback.correct_en: The nominalized clause 'the one at the top' is being set up as the topic, and the sentence then identifies what/who it is. は fits this topic→comment framing.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would present 'the one at the top' as newly spotlighted information, but here the structure is 'as for the one at the top → it was Adachi.' That's a classic は pattern.

contrast_examples.jp: 一位の人は足立だった。
contrast_examples.en: The person in first place was Adachi. (topic→identify)
Adachi was in first place. (new info about who)

prompt.context_jp: 三軒家に初めて会った庭野の視点。
prompt.prompt_jp: 噂どおりの美しさだった___、その顔には笑みの欠片も浮かんでいない。
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the particle that sets up the contrast between beauty and no smile.

feedback.correct_en: Here が works as the conjunction 'but,' linking two clauses that contrast — she was beautiful, BUT she wasn't smiling. This is the connective-が, not the subject-marking one.
feedback.incorrect_en: を and に can't link two independent clauses as 'but.' Only the conjunctive が (or けど) does that work here.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼女は美人だが、冷たい。
contrast_examples.en: She's beautiful, but cold.

contrast_examples.jp: 行きたいが、時間がない。
contrast_examples.en: I'd like to go, but I have no time.

prompt.context_jp: 屋代が「みんなで売ろう」と言った直後の三軒家の宣言。
prompt.prompt_jp: その物件___私が売ります。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle that contrasts this particular property against the group plan.

feedback.correct_en: は fronts 'that property' as a contrastive topic — 'as for that one, I will sell it (not us together).' Pairing は on the object with が on 私 creates the sharp '(particularly) I will sell it' feel.
feedback.incorrect_en: を would be grammatical but neutral; it loses the contrastive punch. が on 物件 would make the property the new subject, which clashes with 私が.

contrast_examples.jp: その件は私がやります。
contrast_examples.en: As for that matter, I'll do it. (contrastive topic + exhaustive 私)

contrast_examples.jp: その件を私がやります。
contrast_examples.en: I'll do that matter. (plainer, no contrastive framing)

prompt.context_jp: 朝礼のあと、営業所がざわつく場面。
prompt.prompt_jp: しかし、新しいチーフの宣言___、誰の頭からも消えてはいなかった。
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the particle that treats the just-mentioned declaration as the topic.

feedback.correct_en: The declaration was just made in the previous paragraph, so it's already established in the discourse. は picks it up as the known topic and comments on its lingering effect.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would present the declaration as fresh new information, but the reader has just read about it — it isn't new anymore.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼女の言葉は、今も耳に残っている。
contrast_examples.en: Her words (already known) still ring in my ears.

contrast_examples.jp: 突然、誰かの声が聞こえた。
contrast_examples.en: Suddenly a voice (new) could be heard.

prompt.context_jp: 三軒家が白洲美加に鍵を取り上げる場面。
prompt.prompt_jp: お客様のアポが取れるまで あなた___家に帰れません。
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the particle for addressing 'you' directly as the topic.

feedback.correct_en: 三軒家 is directly addressing 美加 and setting her up as the topic of the sentence — 'as for you, you can't go home.' That topic framing of a known addressee calls for は.
feedback.incorrect_en: あなたが would turn it into exhaustive 'YOU (as opposed to others) can't go home,' which isn't the point — the point is a general restriction on 美加.

contrast_examples.jp: あなたは今日残業です。
contrast_examples.en: You will be working late today. (statement about you as topic)

contrast_examples.jp: あなたが行くんですか？
contrast_examples.en: Are YOU the one going? (identifying who)

prompt.context_jp: 弥生到着の直後。
prompt.prompt_jp: 庭野___すぐさま駆け寄り、深々と頭を下げた。
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the particle that keeps 庭野 as the ongoing topic.

feedback.correct_en: 庭野 is already a known character actively being tracked by the narrative. は continues him as topic and reports what he did next.
feedback.incorrect_en: 庭野が would suggest someone new was being identified as the one who rushed over, but we already know who he is.

contrast_examples.en: Niwano (ongoing topic) ran right away.

contrast_examples.jp: 誰かが走ってきた。それは庭野だった。
contrast_examples.en: Someone ran up — it was Niwano. (introduction via が)

prompt.context_jp: 弥生がリビングイン階段にこだわる理由を語る場面。
prompt.prompt_jp: リビングイン階段___あれば、子供は必ず リビングを通ってから 2階の自分の部屋に行く。
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the particle inside this conditional clause.

feedback.correct_en: In a conditional subordinate clause like ～があれば, the subject takes が. The clause asserts the mere existence of such stairs as the condition.
feedback.incorrect_en: は inside a conditional ～あれば clause sounds off; は naturally belongs to the main clause topic, not to the if-clause subject.

contrast_examples.en: If I have money, I'll buy it.
Money (topic) is important.

prompt.context_jp: 三軒家が庭野に不動産屋としての心得を語る場面。
prompt.prompt_jp: 不動産屋___地図を見ない。
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the particle that frames 'realtors' as a generic topic.

feedback.correct_en: This is a generic statement about realtors as a category — 'realtors (as a rule) don't look at maps.' Generic category topics take は.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would turn it into 'it's realtors (specifically, exhaustively) who don't look at maps,' which is a different, cleft-like meaning that doesn't fit her teaching here.

contrast_examples.en: Cats like fish. (generic topic)
I like cats. / Cats are what I like.

prompt.context_jp: 小金井夫妻に対する三軒家の宣言。
prompt.prompt_jp: 私の仕事___家を売ることです。
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the particle that defines what her job IS.

feedback.correct_en: This is a classic X は Y です 'definition' pattern — 'as for my job, it is selling houses.' Definitions and identifications take は on the topic.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would mean 'it is MY JOB (not someone else's) that is selling houses,' an exhaustive reading that misses the tone of a self-defining declaration.

contrast_examples.en: My hobby is reading. (definition)
I'm the one who's the section chief. (exhaustive identification)

prompt.context_jp: 屋代が足立のエルメスのネクタイを褒める場面。
prompt.prompt_jp: 何千万もする家___売るんだから それぐらいの演出は必要だな。
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the particle that marks the direct object of 売る.

feedback.correct_en: 売る is transitive — you sell something. The 'something' (expensive houses) is marked by を as the direct object.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would make the houses the subject, which doesn't match 売る here. に would mark a destination/recipient, not the thing being sold.

contrast_examples.en: To sell a house.
A house sells / is sellable. (intransitive)

prompt.context_jp: 三軒家が美加に鍵を要求する場面。
prompt.prompt_jp: 鍵___出しなさい。
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the particle for the thing being handed over.

feedback.correct_en: 出す here means 'take out / hand over,' a transitive verb. 鍵 is what's being produced, so it takes を.
feedback.incorrect_en: 鍵に出す would mean 'put out to the key,' which doesn't make sense. 鍵が出しなさい is ungrammatical as a command.

contrast_examples.en: Take out your wallet.
To take out the trash.

prompt.context_jp: 三軒家の指示。
prompt.prompt_jp: これで 新宿駅___立って 道行く人に物件を営業しなさい。
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the particle marking the location at which she should stand.

feedback.correct_en: With 立つ, に marks the place where someone takes up a position / exists. '駅に立つ' = 'stand (positioned) at the station.'
feedback.incorrect_en: で marks the location of an action/event (駅で働く). But 立つ 'to stand (be positioned)' takes に for the point of location.

contrast_examples.en: Stand on the corner.
Wait at the station. (action location)

prompt.context_jp: 屋代が庭野に自営業客への注意を促す場面。
prompt.prompt_jp: 散々 ___ 結局 売れませんでした なんてことにならないようにな。
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the expression that fits '[getting] jerked around by a client.'

feedback.correct_en: 振り回される = 'to be jerked around / dragged along' — exactly the complaint about a client who keeps you running without closing. It collocates with 散々.
feedback.incorrect_en: 振り向く is 'to turn around (look back)' and 振り返る is 'to look/turn back' — neither captures 'being manipulated/jerked around.'

contrast_examples.en: To be jerked around by a client.

contrast_examples.jp: 名前を呼ばれて振り返る。
contrast_examples.en: To turn around when called.

prompt.context_jp: 三軒家が1518万円という売上額を告げた直後。
prompt.prompt_jp: 営業所の中は、___ように静まり返った。
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the set simile for a dead silence.

feedback.correct_en: 水を打ったよう is the standard idiom for a crowd falling into sudden total silence — 'as if water had been sprinkled (settling the dust).' It's the natural collocation with 静まり返る.
feedback.incorrect_en: 火が消えたよう does describe quiet, but typically liveliness fading rather than sudden shocked silence. 息を止めた isn't a conventional simile here.

contrast_examples.jp: 会場は水を打ったように静まった。
contrast_examples.en: The hall fell dead silent.

contrast_examples.jp: 火が消えたように寂しくなった。
contrast_examples.en: It grew lonely as if a flame had gone out.

prompt.context_jp: できる人がなぜ他営業所から送られてくるのか、を話す場面。
prompt.prompt_jp: いるんだよ そういう営業所___が。
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the word that fits 'office-wrecker / troublemaker.'

feedback.correct_en: 営業所荒らし uses 荒らす 'to ravage/disturb' — someone who storms into an office and shakes things up. It fits the ominous foreshadowing about Sangenya.
feedback.incorrect_en: 営業所育て doesn't exist as a noun. 営業所回り would mean 'making the rounds of offices,' which is just travel, not disruption.

contrast_examples.en: A burglar (ravager of empty houses).
To go out making sales rounds.

prompt.context_jp: 三軒家の決め台詞。
prompt.prompt_jp: 私に___家はありません！
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the form that makes her signature catchphrase.

feedback.correct_en: 売れない is the potential negative — 'cannot be sold.' Her boast is that no house is beyond her ability to sell.
feedback.incorrect_en: 売らない (won't sell) sounds like a refusal of choice, not inability — wrong boast. 売っていない (haven't sold) is a plain state, not a brag.

contrast_examples.jp: 私に書けない字はない。
contrast_examples.en: There's no character I can't write. (potential)
I won't write. (volitional refusal)

prompt.context_jp: 狭い路地で車を曲げる場面。
prompt.prompt_jp: 何度も___を繰り返し、庭野はようやく車を角の向こうへと押し込んだ。
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the word for the back-and-forth maneuvering of a car.

feedback.correct_en: 切り返し is the standard word for repeatedly turning the steering wheel back and forth to maneuver in a tight space — exactly what Niwano is doing.
feedback.incorrect_en: 切り分け is 'cutting apart / dividing' (not driving). 引き返し means 'turning back/retreating' — he isn't retreating, he's wiggling through.

contrast_examples.en: To make a multi-point turn in a narrow road.
To turn back midway.

prompt.context_jp: 屋代が三軒家の指導方法を叱る場面。
prompt.prompt_jp: 君がやってることは___だぞ。
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the word that labels her forced treatment of 美加.

feedback.correct_en: パワハラ = power harassment — abuse by someone in a higher position. Taking a subordinate's house key and forcing her into a sandwich board is a textbook power-position abuse.
feedback.incorrect_en: セクハラ is sexual harassment (not involved here). モラハラ is moral/emotional abuse in close relationships, usually domestic — not quite workplace rank abuse.

contrast_examples.jp: 上司のパワハラが問題だ。
contrast_examples.en: The boss's power harassment is a problem.
A sexually harassing remark.

prompt.context_jp: 弥生が三軒家に対して放つ鋭い一言。
prompt.prompt_jp: 人の___を突いてきて、あなたって何者なの？
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the word that completes 'exploiting someone's vulnerability.'

feedback.correct_en: 弱みを突く is the fixed collocation 'to strike at someone's weak point / exploit a vulnerability.' Sangenya has found exactly what Yayoi is struggling with — childcare.
feedback.incorrect_en: 強みを突く isn't idiomatic — you don't 'attack' someone's strength. 重みを突く doesn't exist as a phrase.

contrast_examples.en: To take advantage of someone's weakness.
To make use of his strengths.

prompt.context_jp: 「王子」と呼ばれる足立の様子。
prompt.prompt_jp: 本人はその呼び名を___もなく、にこやかに上司の視線を受け止めた。
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the pattern meaning 'without even caring about it.'

feedback.correct_en: 〜するでもなく is a set adverbial pattern meaning 'without really doing / without bothering to do.' It conveys mild indifference, perfect for the easygoing Prince.
feedback.incorrect_en: 気にしてもなく is ungrammatical. 気にするにもなく isn't the standard form; the fixed construction is 〜(する)でもなく.

contrast_examples.en: To gaze absently, not really looking.
He laughed, not quite angry.

prompt.context_jp: 三軒家が『みんなで売ろう』の雰囲気を一瞬で断ち切る宣言。
prompt.prompt_en: Which version sounds more like Sangenya's sharp, declarative style?

choices.text: その物件は私が売ります。私に売れない家はありません！
その物件を私も売ろうと思います。売れない家もあるかもしれませんが。

feedback.correct_en: A matches Sangenya's blunt, confident register: 'As for THAT property, I'LL sell it. There is no house I can't sell.' The は/が pairing and the absolute negative are her trademarks.
feedback.incorrect_en: B hedges with 〜も and 〜かもしれません, turning her declaration into tentative teamwork — the opposite of her character.

contrast_examples.jp: この件は私が担当します。
contrast_examples.en: I'll handle this case. (firm, exhaustive)

contrast_examples.jp: この件は私も手伝えればと…。
contrast_examples.en: I'd be glad if I could help with this too... (soft, tentative)

prompt.context_jp: 三軒家が庭野に不動産屋としての教訓を語る場面。
prompt.prompt_en: Which generic maxim phrasing sounds more natural in Japanese?

choices.text: 不動産屋は地図を見ない。
不動産屋が地図を見ない。

feedback.correct_en: Generic truths about a profession use は: 'Realtors (as a rule) don't look at maps.' This is a defining-the-profession statement.
feedback.incorrect_en: B with が sounds like an answer to 'who doesn't look at maps?' — exhaustive identification — which doesn't match a general maxim being offered as advice.

contrast_examples.jp: 医者は患者を見捨てない。
contrast_examples.en: Doctors don't abandon patients. (general truth)
Doctors are in short supply. (new info)

prompt.context_jp: 三軒家が白洲美加に突きつける一文。
prompt.prompt_en: Which word order sounds more natural for the condition-then-consequence?

choices.text: お客様のアポが取れるまで、あなたは家に帰れません。
あなたは家に帰れません、お客様のアポが取れるまで。

feedback.correct_en: Japanese places subordinate time/condition clauses (〜まで) BEFORE the main clause. A follows that neutral order; the condition sets up the consequence.
feedback.incorrect_en: B postposes the 〜まで clause, which can occur in colloquial afterthoughts but sounds unnatural as a formal declaration from a boss.

contrast_examples.en: You can't go home until it's finished.
Postposed version — marked, afterthought feel.

prompt.context_jp: 庭野が「気に入ってくださいました」と報告した時の屋代の叱責。
prompt.prompt_en: Which phrasing sounds more natural as a boss's scolding?

choices.text: 得意げに報告してるようじゃ、プロとはいえないぞ。
嬉しそうに言ってるようじゃ、プロと呼ばない。

feedback.correct_en: 得意げに (looking pleased with yourself) + 〜ようじゃ + プロとはいえない is a tightly idiomatic boss-scold combo. 〜とはいえない 'can't be called' is the standard put-down.
feedback.incorrect_en: B's 嬉しそうに言う is grammatical but weaker; プロと呼ばない (I won't call you a pro) sounds like a personal refusal rather than the general professional-standard judgment the scene wants.

contrast_examples.jp: それじゃプロとはいえない。
contrast_examples.en: At that rate you can't be called a pro.

contrast_examples.jp: それじゃ合格とはいえない。
contrast_examples.en: That can't be called a pass.

prompt.context_jp: 三軒家が小金井夫妻に自己紹介的に放つ一言。
prompt.prompt_en: Which version keeps Sangenya's crisp professional declaration?

choices.text: 私の仕事は家を売ることです。私に売れない家はありません。
私の仕事って家を売ることなんですよね。売れない家ってあんまりないかな。

feedback.correct_en: A uses the clean X は Y です definition pattern and an absolute negative — the register of a confident professional. It matches Sangenya's cool, declarative speech.
feedback.incorrect_en: B's って and 〜かな hedge everything into casual self-talk. That tone would undercut her 'no house I can't sell' persona entirely.

contrast_examples.jp: 私の仕事は家を売ることです。
contrast_examples.en: My job is to sell houses. (crisp)

contrast_examples.jp: 私の仕事ってさ、家売ることなんだよね。
contrast_examples.en: Like, my job is selling houses, y'know. (casual)
